entries.b494a0f2dd56430f00f001246ce6ebf8a2698dfa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv122"/><title type="x-ms">Second Timothy</title> <div sID="gen32480" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32481" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> second epistle Paul wrote to Timothy from Rome, when he was a prisoner there and in danger of his life; this is evident from these words, <hi type="italic">I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6">ch. iv. 6</reference>. It appears that his removal out of this world, in his own apprehension, was not far off, especially considering the rage and malice of his persecutors; and that he had been brought before the emperor Nero, which he calls <hi type="italic">his first answer, when no man stood with him, but all men forsook him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">ch. iv. 16</reference>. And interpreters agree that this was the last epistle he wrote. Where Timothy now was is not certain. The scope of this epistle somewhat differs from that of the former, not so much relating to his office as an evangelist as to his personal conduct and behaviour. <div eID="gen32481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32482" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32483" type="x-p"/> After the introduction (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.1-2Tim.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) we have, I. Paul's sincere love to Timothy, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.3-2Tim.1.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. II. Divers exhortations given to him, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6-2Tim.1.14">ver. 6-14</reference>. III. He speaks of Phygellus and Hermogenes, with others, and closes with Onesiphorus, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.15-2Tim.1.18">ver. 15, to the end</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv122"/> <div eID="gen32483" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32482" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Introduction; Timothy's Faith and Holiness. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32484" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus, 2 To Timothy, <hi type="italic">my</hi> dearly beloved son: Grace, mercy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. 3 I thank God, whom I serve from <hi type="italic">my</hi> forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day; <hi type="super">4</hi> Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy; <hi type="super">5</hi> When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also. <div eID="gen32484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32485" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The inscription of the epistle Paul calls himself <hi type="italic">an apostle by the will of God,</hi> merely by the good pleasure of God, and by his grace, which he professes himself unworthy of. <hi type="italic">According to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus,</hi> or according to the gospel. The gospel is the promise of life in Christ Jesus; life is the end, and Christ the way, <reference osisRef="John.14.6">John xiv. 6</reference>. The life is put into the promise, and both are sure in Christ Jesus the faithful witness; <hi type="italic">for all the promises of God in Christ Jesus are yea, and all amen,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2 Cor. i. 20</reference>. He calls Timothy his <hi type="italic">beloved son.</hi> Paul felt the warmest affection for him both because he had been an instrument of his conversion and because as a son with his father he had served with him in the gospel. Observe, 1. Paul was an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God; as he did not receive the gospel of man, nor was taught it, but had it by the revelation of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.12">Gal. i. 12</reference>), so his commission to be an apostle was not by the will of man, but of God: in the former epistle he says it was <hi type="italic">by the commandment of God our Saviour,</hi> and here <hi type="italic">by the will of God.</hi> God called him to be an apostle. 2. We have the promise of life, blessed be God for it: <hi type="italic">In hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before the world began,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">Tit. i. 2</reference>. It is a promise to discover the freeness and certainty of it. 3. This, as well as all other promises, is in and through Jesus Christ; they all take their rise from the mercy of God in Christ, and they are sure, so that we may safely depend on them. 4. The grace, mercy, and peace, which even Paul's dearly beloved son Timothy wanted, comes from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord; and therefore the one as well as the other is the giver of these blessings, and ought to be applied to for them. 5. The best want these blessings, and they are the best we can ask for our dearly-beloved friends, that they may have grace to help them in the time of need, and mercy to pardon what is amiss, and so may have peace with God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. <div eID="gen32485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32486" type="x-p"/> II. Paul's thanksgiving to God for Timothy's faith and holiness: he thanks God that he remembered Timothy in his prayers. Observe, Whatever good we do, and whatever good office we perform for our friends, God must have the glory of it, and we must give him thanks. It is he who puts it into our hearts to remember such and such in our prayers. Paul was much in prayer, he prayed night and day; in all his prayers he was mindful of his friends, he particularly prayed for good ministers, he prayed for Timothy, and <hi type="italic">had remembrance of him in his prayers night and day;</hi> he did this without ceasing; prayer was his constant business, and he never forgot his friends in his prayers, as we often do. Paul served God from his forefathers with a pure conscience. It was a comfort to him that he was born in God's house, and was of the seed of those that served God; as likewise that he had served him with a pure conscience, according to the best of his light; he had kept a conscience void of offence, and made it his daily exercise to do so, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">Acts xxiv. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">He greatly desired to see Timothy,</hi> out of the affection he had for him, that he might have some conversation with him, <hi type="italic">being mindful of his tears</hi> at their last parting. Timothy was sorry to part with Paul, he wept at parting, and therefore Paul desired to see him again, because he had perceived by that what a true affection he had for him. He thanks God that Timothy kept up the religion of his ancestors, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">v. 5</reference>. Observe, The entail of religion descended upon Timothy by the mother's side; he had a good mother, and a good grandmother: they believed, though his father did not, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Acts xvi. 1</reference>. It is a comfortable thing when children imitate the faith and holiness of their godly parents, and tread in their steps, <reference osisRef="3John.1.4">3 John 4</reference>.—<hi type="italic">Dwelt in thy grandmother and thy mother, and I am persuaded that in thee also.</hi> Paul had a very charitable opinion of his friends, was very willing to hope the best concerning them; indeed he had a great deal of reason to believe well of Timothy, for he had <hi type="italic">no man like-minded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.20">Phil. ii. 20</reference>. Observe, 1. We are, according to St. Paul, to serve God with a pure conscience, so did his and our pious forefathers; this is to draw <hi type="italic">near with a true heart, in full assurance of faith, having our heart sprinkled from an evil conscience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">Heb. x. 22</reference>. 2. In our prayers we are to remember without ceasing our friends, especially the faithful ministers of Christ. Paul had remembrance of his dearly beloved son Timothy in his prayers night and day. 3. The faith that dwells in real believers is unfeigned; it is without hypocrisy, it is a faith that will stand the trial, and it dwells in them as a living principle. It was the matter of Paul's thanksgiving that Timothy inherited the faith of his mother Eunice and his grandmother Lois, and ought to be ours whenever we see the like; we should rejoice wherever we see the grace of God; so did Barnabas, <reference osisRef="Acts.11.23-Acts.11.24">Acts xi. 23, 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">I rejoiced greatly that I found of thy children walking in the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2John.1.4">2 John 4</reference>.
entries.ee359666e77e206da945935e195928b739dcec90: <div eID="gen32486" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions and Exhortations; Ministerial Fidelity. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands. <hi type="super">7</hi> For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind. <hi type="super">8</hi> Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God; <hi type="super">9</hi> Who hath saved us, and called <hi type="italic">us</hi> with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began, <hi type="super">10</hi> But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel: <hi type="super">11</hi> Whereunto I am appointed a preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles. <hi type="super">12</hi> For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. <hi type="super">13</hi> Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">14</hi> That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us. <div eID="gen32487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32488" type="x-p"/> Here is an exhortation and excitation of Timothy to his duty (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I put thee in remembrance.</hi> The best men need remembrancers; what we know we should be reminded of. <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.1">2 Pet. iii. 1</reference>, I write this, <hi type="italic">to stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance.</hi> <div eID="gen32488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32489" type="x-p"/> I. He exhorts him to stir <hi type="italic">up the gift of God</hi> that was <hi type="italic">in him.</hi> Stir it up as fire under the embers. It is meant of all the gifts and graces the God had given him, to qualify him for the work of an evangelist, the gifts of the Holy Ghost, the extraordinary gifts that were conferred by the imposition of the apostle's hands. These he must stir up; he must exercise them and so increase them: use gifts and have gifts. <hi type="italic">To him that hath shall be given,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.29">Matt. xxv. 29</reference>. He must take all opportunities to use these gifts, and so stir them up, for that is the best way of increasing them. Whether the gift of God in Timothy was ordinary or extraordinary (though I incline to the latter), he must stir it up, otherwise it would decay. Further, you see that this gift was in him by the putting on of the apostle's hands, which I take to be distinct from his ordination, for that was performed by the hands of the presbytery, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1 Tim. iv. 14</reference>. It is probable that Timothy had the Holy Ghost, in his extraordinary gifts and graces, conferred on him by the laying on of the apostle's hands (for I reckon that none but the apostles had the power of giving the Holy Ghost), and afterwards, being thus richly furnished for the work of the ministry, was ordained by the presbytery. Observe, 1. The great hindrance of usefulness in the increase of our gifts is slavish fear. Paul therefore warns Timothy against this: <hi type="italic">God hath not given us the spirit of fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">v. 7</reference>. It was through base fear that the evil servant buried his talent, and did not trade with it, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.25">Matt. xxv. 25</reference>. Now God hath therefore armed us against the spirit of fear, by often bidding us fear not. "Fear not the face of man; fear not the dangers you may meet with in the way of your duty." God hath delivered us from the spirit of fear, and hath given us the spirit <hi type="italic">of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.</hi> The spirit of power, or of courage and resolution to encounter difficulties and dangers;—the spirit of love to God, which will carry us through the opposition we may meet with, as Jacob made nothing of the hard service he was to endure for Rachel: the spirit of love to God will set us above the fear of man, and all the hurt that a man can do us;—and the spirit of a sound mind, or quietness of mind, a peaceable enjoyment of ourselves, for we are oftentimes discouraged in our way and work by the creatures o our own fancy and imagination, which a sober, solid, thinking mind would obviate, and would easily answer. 2. The spirit God gives to his ministers is not a fearful, but a courageous spirit; it is a spirit of power, for they speak in his name who has all power, both in heaven and earth; and it is a spirit of love, for love to God and the souls of men must inflame ministers in all their service; and it is a spirit of a sound mind, for they speak the words of truth and soberness. <div eID="gen32489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32490" type="x-p"/> II. He exhorts him to count upon afflictions, and get ready for them: "<hi type="italic">Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner.</hi> Be not thou ashamed of the gospel, of the testimony thou hast borne to it." Observe, <div eID="gen32490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32491" type="x-p"/> 1. The gospel of Christ is what we have none of us reason to be ashamed of. We must not be ashamed of those who are suffering for the gospel of Christ. Timothy must not be ashamed of good old Paul, though he was now in bonds. As he must not himself be afraid of suffering, so he must not be afraid of owning those who were sufferers for the cause of Christ. (1.) The gospel is the testimony of our Lord; in and by this he bears testimony of himself to us, and by professing our adherence to it we bear testimony of him and for him. (2.) Paul was the Lord's prisoner, his prisoner, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Eph. iv. 1</reference>. For his sake he was bound with a chain. (3.) We have no reason to be ashamed either of the testimony of our Lord or of his prisoners; if we are ashamed of either now, Christ will be ashamed of us hereafter. "<hi type="italic">But be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel, according to the power of God,</hi> that is, expect afflictions for the gospel's sake, prepare for them, count upon them, be willing to take thy lot with the suffering saints in this world. <hi type="italic">Be partaker of the afflictions of the gospel;</hi>" or, as it may be read, <hi type="italic">Do thou suffer with the gospel;</hi> "not only sympathize with those who suffer for it, but be ready to suffer with them and suffer like them." If at any time the gospel be in distress, he who hopes for life and salvation by it will be content to suffer with it. Observe, [1.] Then we are likely to bear afflictions as well, when we fetch strength and power from God to enable us to bear them: <hi type="italic">Be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel, according to the power of God.</hi> [2.] All Christians, but especially ministers, must expect afflictions and persecutions for the sake of the gospel. [3.] These shall be proportioned, according to the power of God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>) resting upon us. <div eID="gen32491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32492" type="x-p"/> 2. Mentioning God and the gospel, he takes notice what great things God has done for us by the gospel, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9-2Tim.1.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. To encourage him to suffer, he urges two considerations:— <div eID="gen32492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32493" type="x-p"/> (1.) The nature of that gospel which he was called to suffer for, and the glorious and gracious designs and purposes of it. It is usual with Paul, when he mentions Christ, and the gospel of Christ, to digress from his subject, and enlarge upon them; so full was he of that which is all our salvation, and ought to be all our desire. Observe, [1.] The gospel aims at our salvation: <hi type="italic">He has saved us,</hi> and we must not think much to suffer for that which we hope to be saved by. He has begun to save us, and will complete it in due time; for God calls those things that are not (that are not yet completed) as though they were (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Rom. iv. 17</reference>); therefore he says, who <hi type="italic">has</hi> saved us. [2.] It is designed for our sanctification: <hi type="italic">And called us with a holy calling,</hi> called us to holiness. Christianity is a calling, a holy calling; it is the calling wherewith we are called, the calling to which we are called, to labour in it. Observe, All who shall be saved hereafter are sanctified now. Wherever the call of the gospel is an effectual call, it is found to be a holy call, making those holy who are effectually called. [3.] The origin of it is the free grace and eternal purpose of God in Christ Jesus. If we had merited it, it had been hard to suffer for it; but our salvation by it is of free grace, and not according to our works, and therefore we must not think much to suffer for it. This grace is said to be given us <hi type="italic">before the world began,</hi> that is, in the purpose and designs of God from all eternity; <hi type="italic">in Christ Jesus,</hi> for all the gifts that come from God to sinful man come in and through Christ Jesus. [4.] The gospel is the manifestation of this purpose and grace: <hi type="italic">By the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ,</hi> who had lain in the bosom of the Father from eternity, and was perfectly apprised of all his gracious purposes. By his appearing this gracious purpose was made manifest to us. Did Jesus Christ suffer for it, and shall we think much to suffer for it? [5.] By the gospel of Christ death is abolished: <hi type="italic">He has abolished death,</hi> not only weakened it, but taken it out of the way, has broken the power of death over us; by taking away sin he has abolished death (for the sting of death is sin, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.56">1 Cor. xv. 56</reference>), in altering the property of it, and breaking the power of it. Death now of an enemy has become a friend; it is the gate by which we pass out of a troublesome, vexatious, sinful world, into a world of perfect peace and purity; and the power thereof is broken, for death does not triumph over those who believe the gospel, but they triumph over it. <hi type="italic">O death! where is thy sting? O grave! where is thy victory?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.55">1 Cor. xv. 55</reference>. [6.] He has <hi type="italic">brought life and immortality to light by the gospel;</hi> he has shown us another world more clearly than it was before discovered under any former dispensation, and the happiness of that world, the certain recompence of our obedience by faith: we all with open face, as in a glass, behold the glory of God. He has brought it to light, not only set it before us, but offered it to us, by the gospel. Let us value the gospel more than ever, as it is that whereby life and immortality are brought to light, for herein it has the pre-eminence above all former discoveries; so that it is the gospel of life and immortality, as it discovers them to us, and directs us in the ready way that leads thereto, as well as proposes the most weighty motives to excite our endeavours in seeking after glory, honour, and immortality. <div eID="gen32493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32494" type="x-p"/> (2.) Consider the example of blessed Paul, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.11-2Tim.1.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. He was appointed to preach the gospel, and particularly appointed to teach the Gentiles. He though it a cause worth suffering for, and why should not Timothy think so too? No man needs to be afraid nor ashamed to suffer for the cause of the gospel: <hi type="italic">I am not ashamed,</hi> says Paul, <hi type="italic">for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.</hi> Observe, [1.] Good men often suffer many things for the best cause in the world: <hi type="italic">For which cause I suffer these things;</hi> that is, "for my preaching, and adhering to the gospel." [2.] They need not be ashamed, the cause will bear them out; but those who oppose it shall be clothed with shame. [3.] Those who trust in Christ know whom they have trusted. The apostle speaks with a holy triumph and exultation, as much as to say, "I stand on firm ground. I know I have lodged the great trust in the hands of the best trustee." <hi type="italic">And am persuaded,</hi> &c. What must we commit to Christ? The salvation of our souls, and their preservation to the heavenly kingdom; and what we so commit to him he will keep. There is a day coming when our souls will be enquired after: "Man! Woman! thou hadst a soul committed to thee, what hast thou done with it? To whom it was offered, to God or Satan? How was it employed, in the service of sin or in the service of Christ?" There is a day coming, and it will be a very solemn and awful day, when we must give an account of our stewardship (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.2">Luke xvi. 2</reference>), give an account of our souls: now, if by an active obedient faith we commit it to Jesus Christ, we may be sure he is able to keep it, and it shall be forthcoming to our comfort in that day. <div eID="gen32494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32495" type="x-p"/> III. He exhorts him to <hi type="italic">hold fast the form of sound words,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.13">v. 13</reference>. 1. "<hi type="italic">Have</hi> a form of sound words" (so it may be read), "a short form, a catechism, an abstract of the first principles of religion, according to the scriptures, a scheme of sound words, a brief summary of the Christian faith, in a proper method, drawn out by thyself from the holy scriptures for thy own use;" or, rather, by the form of sound words I understand the holy scriptures themselves. 2. "Having it, <hi type="italic">hold it fast,</hi> remember it, retain it, adhere to it. Adhere to it in opposition to all heresies and false doctrine, which corrupt the Christian faith. Hold that fast <hi type="italic">which thou hast heard of me.</hi>" Paul was divinely inspired. It is good to adhere to those forms of sound words which we have in the scriptures; for these, we are sure, were divinely inspired. That is sound speech, which cannot be condemned, <reference osisRef="Titus.2.8">Tit. ii. 8</reference>. But how must it be held fast? <hi type="italic">In faith and love;</hi> that is, we must assent to it as <hi type="italic">a faithful saying,</hi> and bid it welcome as <hi type="italic">worthy of all acceptation.</hi> Hold it fast in a good heart, this is the ark of the covenant, in which the tables both of law and gospel are most safely and profitably deposited, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.11">Ps. cxix. 11</reference>. Faith and love must go together; it is not enough to believe the sound words, and to give an assent to them, but we must love them, believe their truth and love their goodness, and we must propagate the form of sound words in love; speaking the truth in love, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.15">Eph. iv. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Faith and love which are in Christ Jesus;</hi> it must be Christian faith and love, faith and love fastening upon Jesus Christ, in and by whom God speaks to us and we to him. Timothy, as a minister, must <hi type="italic">hold fast the form of sound words,</hi> for the benefit of others. <hi type="italic">Of healing words,</hi> so it may read; there is healing virtue in the word of God; <hi type="italic">he sent his word, and healed them.</hi> To the same purport is that (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost, which dwelleth in us.</hi> That good thing was the form of sound words, the Christian doctrine, which was committed to Timothy in his baptism and education as he was a Christian, and in his ordination as he was a minister. Observe, (1.) The Christian doctrine is a trust committed to us. It is committed to Christians in general, but to ministers in particular. It is a good thing, of unspeakable value in itself, and which will be of unspeakable advantage to us; it is a good thing indeed, it is an inestimable jewel, for it discovers to us the unsearchable riches of Christ, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Eph. iii. 8</reference>. It is committed to us to be preserved pure and entire, and to be transmitted to those who shall come after us, and we must keep it, and not contribute any thing to the corrupting of its purity, the weakening of its power, or the diminishing of its perfection: <hi type="italic">Keep it by the Holy Ghost that dwelleth in us.</hi> Observe, Even those who are ever so well taught cannot keep what they have learned, any more than they could at first learn it, without the assistance of the Holy Spirit. We must not think to keep it by our own strength, but keep it by the Holy Ghost. (2.) The Holy Ghost dwells in all good ministers and Christians; they are his temples, and he enables them to keep the gospel pure and uncorrupt; and yet they must use their best endeavours to keep this good thing, for the assistance and indwelling of the Holy Ghost do not exclude men's endeavours, but they very well consist together.
entries.fd06990cd8ac563965e1e55bfe04684d9f86a565: <div eID="gen32495" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ministerial Fortitude. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32496" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> This thou knowest, that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me; of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes. 16 The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain: <hi type="super">17</hi> But, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found <hi type="italic">me.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day: and in how many things he ministered unto me at Ephesus, thou knowest very well. <div eID="gen32496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32497" type="x-p"/> Having (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.13-2Tim.1.14">v. 13, 14</reference>) exhorted Timothy to hold fast, <div eID="gen32497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32498" type="x-p"/> I. He mentions the apostasy of many from the doctrine of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.15">v. 15</reference>. It seems, in the best and purest ages of the church, there were those that had embraced the Christian faith, and yet afterwards revolted from it, nay, there were many such. He does not say that they had turned away from the doctrine of Christ (though it should seem they had) but they had turned away from him, they had turned their backs upon him, and disowned him in the time of his distress. And should we wonder at it, when many turned their backs on a much better than Paul? I mean the Lord Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="John.6.66">John vi. 66</reference>. <div eID="gen32498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32499" type="x-p"/> II. He mentions the constancy of one that adhered to him, namely, Onesiphorus: <hi type="italic">For he often refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16">v. 16</reference>. Observe, 1. What kindness Onesiphorus had shown to Paul: he refreshed him, he often refreshed him with his letters, and counsels, and comforts, and he was not ashamed of his chains. He was not ashamed of him, not withstanding the disgrace he was now under. He was kind to him not once or twice, but often; not only when he was at Ephesus among his own friends, but when Onesiphorus was at Rome; he took care to seek Paul <hi type="italic">out very diligently, and found him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.17">v. 17</reference>. Observe, A good man will seek opportunities of doing good, and will not shun any that offer. At Ephesus he had ministered to him, and been very kind to him: Timothy knew it. 2. How Paul returns his kindness, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16-2Tim.1.18">v. 16-18</reference>. He that receives a prophet shall have a prophet's reward. He repays him with his prayers: <hi type="italic">The Lord give mercy to Onesiphorus.</hi> It is probable that Onesiphorus was now absent from home, and in company with Paul; Paul therefore prays that his house might be kept during his absence. Though the papists will have it that he was now dead; and, from Paul's praying for him that he might find mercy, they conclude the warrantableness of praying for the dead; but who told them that Onesiphorus was dead? And can it be safe to ground a doctrine and practice of such importance on a mere supposition and very great uncertainty? <div eID="gen32499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32500" type="x-p"/> III. He prays for Onesiphorus himself, as well as for his house: <hi type="italic">That he may find mercy in that day,</hi> in the day of death and of judgment, when Christ will account all the good offices done to his poor members as done to himself. Observe, 1. The day of death and judgment is an awful day, and may be emphatically called <hi type="italic">that day.</hi> 2. We need desire no more to make us happy than to find mercy of the Lord in that day, when those that have shown no mercy will have judgment without mercy. 3. The best Christians will want mercy in that day; <hi type="italic">looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.21">Jude 21</reference>. 4. If you would have mercy then, you must seek for it now of the Lord. 5. It is of and from the Lord that we must have mercy; for, unless the Lord has mercy on us, in vain will be the pity and compassion of men or angels. 6. We are to seek and ask for mercy of the Lord, who is the giver and bestower of it; for the Lord Jesus Christ has satisfied justice, that mercy might be displayed. We are to come to a throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in the time of need. 7. The best thing we can seek, either for ourselves or our friends, is that the Lord will grant to them that they may find mercy of the Lord in that day, when they must pass our of time into eternity, and exchange this world for the other, and appear before the judgment-seat of Christ: the Lord then grant unto all of us that we may find mercy of the Lord in that day.  <chapter eID="2Tim.1"/> <div eID="gen32500" type="x-p"/>

entries.ec46ded382fc347acf37a053fd757940787c8c56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18168"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen37527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Place of Writing.--</hi>Paul, in the interval between his first and second imprisonment, after having written First Timothy from Macedonia or Corinth [Birks] (if we are to adopt the opinion that First Timothy was written after his first imprisonment), returned to Ephesus, as he intended, by way of Troas, where he left the books, &c. (mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">2Ti 4:13</reference>), with Carpus. From Ephesus he went to Crete for a short visit and returned, and then wrote to Titus. Next he went by Miletus to Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>), and thence to Nicopolis (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>), whence he proceeded to Rome. From his prison there he wrote the Second Epistle to Timothy, shortly before his martyrdom. It is not certain where Timothy was at this time. Some of the internal evidences favor the view of his having been then at Ephesus; thus the salutation of Priscilla and Aquila, who generally resided there (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.19">2Ti 4:19</reference>); also that of the household of Onesiphorus, who is stated in <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16-2Tim.1.18">2Ti 1:16-18</reference> to have ministered to Paul at Ephesus, a circumstance implying his residence there. Also, the Hymenæus of <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference> seems to be the same as the Hymenæus at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>); and probably "Alexander the coppersmith" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.14">2Ti 4:14</reference>) is the same as the Alexander joined with Hymenæus (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>), and possibly the same as the Alexander put forward by the Jews to clear themselves, not to befriend Paul, at the riot in Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.33">Ac 19:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.34">34</reference>). The difficulty is, on this supposition, how to account for <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">20</reference>: if Timothy was at Ephesus, why did he need to be told that Paul had sent Tychicus to Ephesus? or that Paul had left Trophimus, himself an Ephesian (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.29">Ac 21:29</reference>), sick at Miletus, which was only thirty miles from Ephesus? However, see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>. Troas lay on the road to Rome from either Ephesus or Pontus, so that <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">2Ti 4:13</reference> will accord with the theory of either Ephesus or any other place in the northwest of Asia Minor, being Timothy's place of sojourn at the time. Probably, he had the general superintendence of the Pauline churches in Asia Minor, in accordance with his mission combining the office of evangelist, or itinerant missionary, with that of presiding overseer. Ephesus was probably his headquarters.<div eID="gen37527" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37526" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Time of Writing.--</hi>(1) Paul's first imprisonment, described in <reference osisRef="Acts.28.17-Acts.28.31">Ac 28:17-31</reference>, was much milder than that in which he was when writing Second Timothy. In the former, he had liberty to lodge in his own hired house, and to receive all comers, guarded only by a single soldier; in the latter, he was so closely confined that Onesiphorus with difficulty found him; he was chained, his friends had forsaken him, and he had narrowly escaped sentence of execution from the Roman emperor. Medieval legends represent the Mamertine prison, or Tullianum, as the scene of his incarceration with Peter. But this is irreconcilable with the fact of Onesiphorus, Linus, Pudens, &c., having access to him. He was probably under military custody, as in his former imprisonment, though of a severer kind (2Ti 1:16-18; 2:9; 4:6-8, 16, 17). (2) The visit to Troas (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">2Ti 4:13</reference>) can hardly have been that mentioned in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.5-Acts.20.7">Ac 20:5-7</reference>, the last before his first imprisonment; for, if it were, the interval between that visit and the first imprisonment would be seven or eight years, a period most unlikely for him to have allowed to pass without sending for his cloak and parchments, when they might have been of service to him in the interim. (3) Paul's leaving Trophimus sick at Miletus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>), could not have been on the occasion mentioned in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.15">Ac 20:15</reference>; for, subsequent to that, Trophimus was with Paul in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.29">Ac 21:29</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.4">4</reference>) The words (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>), "Erastus abode at Corinth," imply that Paul had shortly before been at Corinth, where he left Erastus. But before his first imprisonment, Paul had not been at Corinth for several years; and in the interval Timothy had been with him, so that Timothy did not need at a later period to be told about that visit (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.2">Ac 20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">4</reference>). For all these reasons the imprisonment, during which he wrote Second Timothy, is shown to be his second imprisonment. Moreover, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.23">He 13:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.24">24</reference>, represents the writer (who was probably Paul) as in Italy, and at liberty. So Clement of Rome [First Epistle to the Corinthians, 1.5], the disciple of Paul, explicitly states, "In the east and west, Paul as a preacher instructed the whole world (that is, the Roman empire) in righteousness, and having gone to the extremity of the west, and having borne witness before the rulers (of Rome), he so was removed from the world." This plainly implies that he fulfilled his design (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.24-Rom.15.28">Ro 15:24-28</reference>) of a missionary journey into Spain. The canon of the New Testament, compiled about A.D. 170 (called Muratori's Canon), also mentions "the journey of Paul from Rome to Spain." See Routh [Sacred Fragments, vol. 4, p. 1-12].<div eID="gen37528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37529" type="x-p"/> His martyrdom is universally said to have occurred in Nero's reign [Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 2.22; Jerome, On Illustrious Men]. Five years thus seem to have elapsed between the first imprisonment, A.D. 63 (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.17-Acts.28.31">Ac 28:17-31</reference>), and his martyrdom, June A.D. 68, the last year of Nero's reign. He was probably arrested by the magistrates in Nicopolis (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>) in Epirus, in the winter, on a double charge, first, of being one of the Christians who had conspired, it was alleged by Nero's partisans, to set fire to Rome, A.D. 64; secondly, of introducing a novel and unlawful religion. His friends all left him, except Luke: Demas from "love of this present world": the others from various causes (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">11</reference>). On the first charge he seems to have been acquitted. His liberation from his first imprisonment took place in A.D. 63, the year before the great fire at Rome, which Nero made the pretext for his persecution of the Christians. Every cruelty was heaped on them; some were crucified; some were arrayed in the skins of wild beasts and hunted to death by dogs; some were wrapped in pitch-robes and set on fire by night to illuminate the circus of the Vatican and gardens of Nero, while that monster mixed among the spectators in the garb of a charioteer. But now (A.D. 67 or 68) some years had elapsed since the first excitement which followed the fire. Hence, Paul, being a Roman citizen, was treated in his trial with a greater respect for the forms of the law, and hence was acquitted (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>) on the first charge of having instigated the Christians to their supposed acts of incendiarism before his last departure from Rome. Alexander the coppersmith seems to have been a witness against him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.14">2Ti 4:14</reference>). Had he been condemned on the first charge, he would probably have been burnt alive, as the preceding martyrs were, for arson. His judge was the city Præfect. Clement of Rome specifies that his trial was (not before the emperor, but) "before the rulers." No advocate ventured to plead his cause, no patron appeared for him, such as under ordinary circumstances might have aided him; for instance, one of the powerful Æmilian house, under which his family possibly enjoyed clientship (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2Ti 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">17</reference>), whence he may have taken his name Paul. The place of trial was, probably, one of the great basilicas in the Forum, two of which were called the Pauline Basilicas, from L. Æmilius Paulus, who had built one and restored the other. He was remanded for the second stage of his trial. He did not expect this to come on until the following "winter" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2Ti 4:21</reference>), whereas it took place about midsummer; if in Nero's reign, not later than June. In the interim Luke was his only constant companion; but one friend from Asia, Onesiphorus, had diligently sought him and visited him in prison, undeterred by the danger. Linus, too, the future bishop of Rome, Pudens, the son of a senator, and Claudia, his bride, perhaps the daughter of a British king (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2Ti 4:21</reference>), were among his visitors; and Tychicus, before he was sent by Paul to Ephesus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:12</reference>; perhaps bearing with him this Epistle).<div eID="gen37529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Object of the epistle.--</hi>He was anxious to see his disciple Timothy, before his death, and that Timothy should bring Mark with him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.4">2Ti 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.21">11, 21</reference>). But feeling how uncertain it was whether Timothy should arrive in time, he felt it necessary, also, to give him by letter a last warning as to the heresies, the germs of which were then being scattered in the Churches. Hence he writes a series of exhortations to faithfulness, and zeal for sound doctrine, and patience amidst trials: a charge which Timothy seems to have needed, if we are to judge from the apostle's earnestness in urging him to boldness in Christ's cause, as though Paul thought he saw in him some signs of constitutional timidity (2Ti 2:2-8; 4:1-5; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1Ti 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen37530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Paul's Death.--</hi>Dioysius, bishop of Corinth (quoted in Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 2.25]) about A.D. 170, is the earliest authority for the tradition that Peter suffered martyrdom at Rome "about the same time" as Paul, after having labored for some time there. He calls Peter and Paul "the founders of the Corinthian and Roman Churches." The Roman presbyter, Caius (about A.D. 200), mentions the tradition that Peter suffered martyrdom in the Vatican. But (1) Peter's work was among the Jews (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Ga 2:9</reference>), whereas Rome was a Gentile Church (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.13">Ro 1:13</reference>. Moreover, (2) the First Epistle of Peter (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1Pe 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.13">5:13</reference>) represents him as laboring in Babylon in Mesopotamia. (3) The silence concerning Peter of Paul's Epistles written in Rome, negatives the tradition of his having founded, or labored long at Rome; though it is possible he may have endured martyrdom there. His martyrdom, certainly, was not, as Jerome says, "on the same day" with that of Paul, else Paul would have mentioned Peter's being at Rome in <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>. The legend says that Peter, through fear, was fleeing from Rome at early dawn by the Appian Way, when he met our Lord, and falling at His feet, asked, Lord, whither goest thou? to which the Lord replied, I go again to be crucified. The disciple returned penitent and ashamed, and was martyred. The Church of Domine quo vadis, on the Appian Way, commemorates the supposed fact. Paul, according to Caius (quoted in Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 2.25]), suffered martyrdom on the Ostian Way. So also Jerome, who gives the date, the fourteenth year of Nero. It was common to send prisoners, whose death might attract too much notice at Rome, to some distance from the city, under a military escort, for execution; hence the soldier's sword, not the executioner's axe, was the instrument of his decapitation [Orosius, The Seven Books of History against the Pagans, 7.7]. Paul appears, from <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12-Phil.1.30">Php 1:12-30</reference>, to have had his partisans even in the palace, and certainly must have exercised such an influence as would excite sympathy in his behalf, to avoid which the execution was ordered outside the city. Compare Tacitus [Histories, 4.11]. The Basilica of St. Paul, first built by Constantine, now stands outside Rome on the road to Ostia: before the Reformation it was under the protection of the kings of England, and the emblem of the order of the Garter is still to be seen among its decorations. The traditional spot of the martyrdom is the Tre Fontane, not far from the Basilica [Conybeare and Howson].<div eID="gen37531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37532" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.1-2Tim.1.18">2Ti 1:1-18</reference>. Address: Thankful Expression of Love and Desire to See Him: Remembrance of His Faith and That of His Mother and Grandmother. Exhortation to Stir Up the Gift of God in Him, and Not Shrink from Affliction, Enforced by the Consideration of the Freeness of God's Grace in Our Gospel Calling, and by the Apostle's Example. The Defection of Many: The Steadfastness of Onesiphorus.<div eID="gen37532" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <div sID="gen37533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18168"/>1. This Epistle is the last testament and swan-like death song of Paul [Bengel].<div eID="gen37533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the promise of life ... in Christ--</hi>Paul's apostleship is in order to carry into effect this promise. Compare "according to the faith ... in hope of eternal life ... promise," &c. (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.1">Tit 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>). This "promise of life in Christ" (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.8">2Ti 2:8</reference>) was needed to nerve Timothy to fortitude amidst trials, and to boldness in undertaking the journey to Rome, which would be attended with much risk (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>). <div eID="gen37534" type="x-p"/>
entries.429e4d50665bdc7e6734bd2c848cc426864b688b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18169"/><div sID="gen37535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18169"/><hi type="bold">2. my dearly beloved son--</hi>In <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Ti 1:2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Titus.1.4">Tit 1:4</reference>, written at an earlier period than this Epistle, the expression used is in the Greek, "my genuine son." Alford sees in the change of expression an intimation of an altered tone as to Timothy, more of mere love, and less of confidence, as though Paul saw m him a want of firmness, whence arose the need of his stirring up afresh the faith and grace in Him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference>). But this seems to me not justified by the Greek word agapetos, which implies the attachment of reasoning and choice, on the ground of merit in the one "beloved," not of merely instinctive love. See Trench [Greek Synonyms of the New Testament]. <div eID="gen37535" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a7ebad007b3c93b35bfa0cb774272f29752be2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18170"/><div sID="gen37536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18170"/><hi type="bold">3. I thank--</hi>Greek, "I feel gratitude to God."<div eID="gen37536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom I serve from my forefathers--</hi>whom I serve (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Ro 1:9</reference>) as did my forefathers. He does not mean to put on the same footing the Jewish and Christian service of God; but simply to assert his own conscientious service of God as he had received it from his progenitors (not Abraham, Isaac, &c., whom he calls "the fathers," not "progenitors" as the Greek is here; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Ro 9:5</reference>). The memory of those who had gone before to whom he is about to be gathered, is now, on the eve of death, pleasant to him; hence also, he calls to mind the faith of the mother and grandmother of Timothy; as he walks in the faith of his forefathers (<reference osisRef="Acts.23.1">Ac 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.14">24:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.6">26:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.20">28:20</reference>), so Timothy should persevere firmly in the faith of his parent and grandparent. Not only Paul, but the Jews who reject Christ, forsake the faith of their forefathers, who looked for Christ; when they accept Him, the hearts of the children shall only be returning to the faith of their forefathers (Mal 4:6; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Lu 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.23">Ro 11:23</reference>, 24, 28). Probably Paul had, in his recent defense, dwelt on this topic, namely, that he was, in being a Christian, only following his hereditary faith.<div eID="gen37537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ... I have remembrance of thee--</hi>"how unceasing I make my mention concerning thee" (compare Phm 4). The cause of Paul's feeling thankful is, not that he remembers Timothy unceasingly in his prayers, but for what Timothy is in faith (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Ti 1:5</reference>) and graces; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.8">Ro 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>, from which supply the elliptical sentence thus, "I thank God (for thee, for God is my witness) whom I serve ... that (or how) without ceasing I have remembrance (or make mention) of thee," &c.<div eID="gen37538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night and day--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.5">1Ti 5:5</reference>). <div eID="gen37539" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c87a63f81dfaedd3c5ed50cf0232ce10e90046a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18171"/><div sID="gen37540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18171"/><hi type="bold">4. desiring--</hi>Greek, "with yearning as for one much missed."<div eID="gen37540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mindful of thy tears--</hi>not only at our parting (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.37">Ac 20:37</reference>), but also often when under pious feelings.<div eID="gen37541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I may be filled with joy--</hi>to be joined with "desiring to see thee" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.11">Ro 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">15:32</reference>). <div eID="gen37542" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a124cbd6b9ce8350b693c40cc5f4c02d45b3569: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18172"/><div sID="gen37543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18172"/><hi type="bold">5. When I call to remembrance--</hi>This increased his "desire to see" Timothy. The oldest manuscripts read, "When I called to remembrance"; implying that some recent incident (perhaps the contrasted cowardice of the hypocrite Demas, who forsook him) had reminded him of the sincerity of Timothy's faith.<div eID="gen37543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faith that is in thee--</hi>Alford translates, "that was in thee." He remembers Timothy's faith in the past as a fact; its present existence in him is only matter of his confident persuasion or hope.<div eID="gen37544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>Greek, "such as."<div eID="gen37545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelt--</hi>"made its dwelling" or abode (<reference osisRef="John.14.23">Joh 14:23</reference>). The past tense implies they were now dead.<div eID="gen37546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first--</hi>before it dwelt in thee. She was the furthest back of the progenitors of Timothy whom Paul knew.<div eID="gen37547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mother Eunice--</hi>a believing Jewess; but his father was a Greek, that is, a heathen (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>). The faith of the one parent sanctified the child (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.14">1Co 7:14</reference>). She was probably converted at Paul's first visit to Lystra (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.6">Ac 14:6</reference>). It is an undesigned coincidence, and so a mark of truth, that in <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference> the belief of the mother alone is mentioned, just as here praise is bestowed on the faith of the mother, while no notice is taken of the father [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ].<div eID="gen37548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>Greek, "but," that is, notwithstanding appearances [Alford].<div eID="gen37549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">persuaded that--</hi>it dwells, or it shall dwell "in thee also." The mention of the faith of his mother and grandmother is designed as an incentive to stir up his faith. <div eID="gen37550" type="x-p"/>
entries.df1bb265d0d13deffd4ce2b132bc2ec6270c802e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18173"/><div sID="gen37551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18173"/><hi type="bold">6. Wherefore--</hi>Greek, "For which cause," namely, because thou hast inherited, didst once possess, and I trust ("am persuaded") still dost possess, such unfeigned faith [Alford].<div eID="gen37551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stir up--</hi>literally, "rekindle," "revive the spark of"; the opposite of "quench" or "extinguish" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.19">1Th 5:19</reference>). Paul does not doubt the existence of real faith in Timothy, but he desires it to be put into active exercise. Timothy seems to have become somewhat remiss from being so long without Paul (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2Ti 2:22</reference>).<div eID="gen37552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gift of God--</hi>the spiritual grace received for his ministerial office, either at his original ordination, or at his consecration to the particular office of superintending the Ephesian Church (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference>), imparting fearlessness, power, love, and a sound mind (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Ti 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen37553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the putting on of my hands--</hi>In <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference>, it is "with [not by] the laying on of the hands of the presbytery." The apostle was chief in the ordination, and to him "BY" is applied. The presbytery were his assistants; so "with," implying merely accompaniment, is said of them. Paul was the instrument in Timothy's ordination and reception of the grace then conferred; the presbyters were the concurrent participants in the act of ordination; so the Greek, "dia" and "meta." So in ordinations by a bishop in our days, he does the principal act; they join in laying on hands with him. <div eID="gen37554" type="x-p"/>
entries.828e82427ddab07df93ae2be2d43becd0910e500: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18174"/><div sID="gen37555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18174"/><hi type="bold">7. For, &c.--</hi>implying that Timothy needed the exhortation "to stir up the gift of God in him," being constitutionally "timid": "For God did not give us (so the Greek, namely, at our ordination or consecration) the spirit of fear." The spirit which He gave us, was not the spirit of timidity (literally, "cowardice," which is weakness), but of "power" (exhibited in a fearless "testimony" for Christ, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>). "Power is the invariable accompaniment of the gift of the Holy Ghost. <reference osisRef="Luke.24.49">Lu 24:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.8">Ac 1:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.6.6">Ac 6:6</reference>, "full of faith and of the Holy Ghost," with <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>, "full of faith and power." Fear is the result of "the spirit of bondage" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Ro 8:15</reference>). Fear within exaggerates the causes of fear without. "The spirit of power" is the spirit of man dwelt in by the Spirit of God imparting power; this power "casteth out fear" from ourselves, and stimulates us to try to cast it out of others (<reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen37555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love--</hi>which moves the believer while "speaking the truth" with power, when giving his testimony for Christ (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>), at the same time to do so "in love" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.15">Ep 4:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a sound mind--</hi>The Greek, is rather, "the bringing of men to a sound mind" [Wahl]. Bengel supports English Version, "a sound mind," or "sober-mindedness"; a duty to which a young man like Timothy especially needed to be exhorted (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2Ti 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.4">Tit 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.6">6</reference>). So Paul urges him, in <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.4">2Ti 2:4</reference>, to give up worldly entanglements, which as thorns (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.14">Lu 8:14</reference>) choke the word. These three gifts are preferable to any miraculous powers whatever. <div eID="gen37557" type="x-p"/>
entries.960e9ccbebc75b96a53079e0db0f32983e4412c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18175"/><div sID="gen37558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18175"/><hi type="bold">8. therefore--</hi>seeing that God hath given us such a spirit, not that of fear.<div eID="gen37558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Be not thou ... ashamed--</hi>I agree with Ellicott, in opposition to Alford, that the Greek subjunctive here, with the negative, implies action completed at one time, not continued action, which the present imperative would express; thus implying that Timothy had not decidedly yet evinced such feeling of shame; though I think, Paul, amidst the desertion of others who once promised fair, and from being aware of Timothy's constitutional timidity (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Ti 1:7</reference>), felt it necessary to stir him up and guard him against the possibility of unchristian dereliction of duty as to bold confession of Christ. Shame (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>) is the companion of fear (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Ti 1:7</reference>); if fear be overcome, false shame flees [Bengel]. Paul himself (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2Ti 1:12</reference>), and Onesiphorus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16">2Ti 1:16</reference>), were instances of fearless profession removing false shame. He presents in contrast sad instances of fear and shame (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.15">2Ti 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the testimony of our Lord--</hi>of the testimony which thou art bound to give in the cause of our Lord; he says "our," to connect Timothy and himself together in the testimony which both should give for their common Lord. The testimony which Christ gave before Pilate (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">1Ti 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">13</reference>), is an incentive to the believer that he should, after His Lord's example, witness a good testimony or confession.<div eID="gen37560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor of me his prisoner--</hi>The cause of God's servants is the cause of God Himself (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>). Timothy might easily be tempted to be ashamed of one in prison, especially as not only worldly shame, but great risk, attended any recognition of Paul the prisoner.<div eID="gen37561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be thou partaker--</hi>with me.<div eID="gen37562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37563" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the gospel--</hi>rather, as Greek, "for the Gospel," that is, suffered for the Gospel (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3-2Tim.2.5">2Ti 2:3-5</reference>; Phm 13).<div eID="gen37563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to the power of God--</hi>exhibited in having saved and called us (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>). God who has done the greater act of power (that is, saved us), will surely do the less (carry us safe through afflictions borne for the Gospel). "Think not that thou hast to bear these afflictions by thine own power; nay, it is by the power of God. It was a greater exercise of power than His making the heaven, His persuading the world to embrace salvation" [Chrysostom]. <div eID="gen37564" type="x-p"/>
entries.e92ae9bf5bff694fafd9eddd9fa9044928d5a00d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18176"/><div sID="gen37565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18176"/><hi type="bold">9. Who ... called us--</hi>namely, God the Father (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.6">Ga 1:6</reference>). The having "saved us" in His eternal purpose of "grace, given us in Christ before the world began," precedes his actual "calling" of us in due time with a call made effective to us by the Holy Spirit; therefore, "saved us" comes before "called us" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.28-Rom.8.30">Ro 8:28-30</reference>).<div eID="gen37565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy calling--</hi>the actual call to a life of holiness. <reference osisRef="Heb.3.1">He 3:1</reference>, "heavenly calling" [Tittmann, Greek Synonyms of the New Testament]; whereas we were sinners and enemies (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>). The call comes wholly from God and claims us wholly for God. "Holy" implies the separation of believers from the rest of the world unto God.<div eID="gen37566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not according to--</hi>not having regard to our works in His election and calling of grace (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.11">Ro 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Ep 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen37567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his own purpose--</hi>The origination of salvation was of His own purpose, flowing from His own goodness, not for works of ours coming first, but wholly because of His own gratuitous, electing love [Theodoret and Calvin].<div eID="gen37568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace ... given us--</hi>in His everlasting purpose, regarded as the same as when actually accomplished in due time.<div eID="gen37569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ--</hi>believers being regarded by God as IN Him, with whom the Father makes the covenant of salvation (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">3:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37571" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the world began--</hi>Greek, "before the times (periods) of ages"; the enduring ages of which no end is contemplated (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.11">Ep 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen37571" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba22e17d60e152ec8871394287d5c4d150f8a882: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18177"/><div sID="gen37572" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18177"/><hi type="bold">10. But ... now ... manifest--</hi>in contrast to its concealment heretofore in the eternal purpose of God "before the world began" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">Tit 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen37572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appearing--</hi>the visible manifestation in the flesh.<div eID="gen37573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abolished death--</hi>Greek, "taken away the power from death" [Tittmann]. The Greek article before "death" implies that Christ abolished death, not only in some particular instance, but in its very essence, being, and idea, as well as in all its aspects and consequences (<reference osisRef="John.11.26">Joh 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Ro 8:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">38</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.26">1Co 15:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.55">55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>). The carrying out of the abolition of death into full effect is to be at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.14">Re 20:14</reference>). The death of the body meanwhile is but temporary, and is made no account of by Christ and the apostles.<div eID="gen37574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought ... to light--</hi>making visible by the Gospel what was before hidden in God's purpose.<div eID="gen37575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">life--</hi>of the Spirit, acting first on the soul here, about to act on the body also at the resurrection.<div eID="gen37576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">immortality--</hi>Greek, "incorruptibility" of the new life, not merely of the risen body [Alford], (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>by means of the Gospel, which brings to light the life and immortality purposed by God from eternity, but manifested now first to man by Christ, who in His own resurrection has given the pledge of His people's final triumph over death through Him. Before the Gospel revelation from God, man, by the light of nature, under the most favorable circumstances, had but a glimmering idea of the possibility of a future being of the soul, but not the faintest idea of the resurrection of the body (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.18">Ac 17:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.32">32</reference>). If Christ were not "the life," the dead could never live; if He were not the resurrection, they could never rise; had He not the keys of hell and death (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Re 1:18</reference>), we could never break through the bars of death or gates of hell [Bishop Pearson]. <div eID="gen37578" type="x-p"/>
entries.51a9289180b62910a7a1c41766bd256b1effd319: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18178"/><div sID="gen37579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18178"/><hi type="bold">11. Whereunto--</hi>For the publication of which Gospel.<div eID="gen37579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am appointed--</hi>Greek, "I was appointed."<div eID="gen37580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preacher--</hi>Greek, "herald."<div eID="gen37581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teacher of the Gentiles--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.7">1Ti 2:7</reference>). He brings forward his own example in this verse and <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2Ti 1:12</reference>, as a pattern for Timothy, as a public "preacher," an "apostle," or missionary from place to place, and a "teacher" in private instructing His flock with patient perseverance. <div eID="gen37582" type="x-p"/>
entries.053df69e0fc6c7d245f3d00ab879eebcc74129dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18179"/><div sID="gen37583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18179"/><hi type="bold">12. For the which cause--</hi>For the Gospel cause of which I was appointed a preacher (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen37583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I also suffer--</hi>besides my active work as a missionary. Ellicott translates, "I suffer even these things"; the sufferings attendant on my being a prisoner (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen37584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am not ashamed--</hi>neither be thou (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.8">2Ti 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen37585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>Confidence as to the future drives away shame [Bengel].<div eID="gen37586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I know--</hi>though the world knows Him not (<reference osisRef="John.10.14">Joh 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.25">17:25</reference>).<div eID="gen37587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom--</hi>I know what a faithful, promise-keeping God He is (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.13">2Ti 2:13</reference>). It is not, I know how I have believed, but, I know WHOM I have believed; a feeble faith may clasp a strong Saviour.<div eID="gen37588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believed--</hi>rather, "trusted"; carrying out the metaphor of a depositor depositing his pledge with one whom he trusts.<div eID="gen37589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">am persuaded--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>).<div eID="gen37590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is able--</hi>in spite of so many foes around me.<div eID="gen37591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which I have committed unto him--</hi>Greek, "my deposit"; the body, soul, and spirit, which I have deposited in God's safe keeping (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.19">1Pe 4:19</reference>). So Christ Himself in dying (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.46">Lu 23:46</reference>). "God deposits with us His word; we deposit with God our spirit" [Grotius]. There is one deposit (His revelation) committed by God to us, which we ought to keep (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.13">2Ti 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>) and transmit to others (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">2Ti 2:2</reference>); there is another committed by God to us, which we should commit to His keeping, namely, ourselves and our heavenly portion.<div eID="gen37592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37593" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that day--</hi>the day of His appearing (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.18">2Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). <div eID="gen37593" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb898d14cf3d63d861a5e6769f9e9730236e549a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18180"/><div sID="gen37594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18180"/><hi type="bold">13. Hold fast the form--</hi>rather as Greek, "Have (that is, keep) a pattern of sound (Greek, 'healthy') words which thou hast heard from me, in faith and love." "Keep" suits the reference to a deposit in the context. The secondary position of the verb in the Greek forbids our taking it so strongly as English Version, "Hold fast." The Greek for "form" is translated "pattern" in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">1Ti 1:16</reference>, the only other passage where it occurs. Have such a pattern drawn from my sound words, in opposition to the unsound doctrines so current at Ephesus, vividly impressed (Wahl translates it "delineation"; the verb implies "to make a lively and lasting impress") on thy mind.<div eID="gen37594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in faith and love--</hi>the element IN which my sound words had place, and in which thou art to have the vivid impression of them as thy inwardly delineated pattern, moulding conformably thy outward profession. So nearly Bengel explains, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.9">1Ti 3:9</reference>. <div eID="gen37595" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec829522850e9aacb6c3a61fe476c729e7a93249: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18181"/><div sID="gen37596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18181"/>14. Translate as Greek, "That goodly deposit keep through the Holy Ghost," namely, "the sound words which I have committed to thee" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.13">2Ti 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">2Ti 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen37596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37597" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in us--</hi>in all believers, not merely in you and me. The indwelling Spirit enables us to keep from the robbers of the soul the deposit of His word committed to us by God. <div eID="gen37597" type="x-p"/>
entries.1acdc497753389a9d61ecffbd29c485d56fefa68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18182"/><div sID="gen37598" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18182"/><hi type="bold">15. all they which are in Asia--</hi>Proconsular Asia; "all who are there now, when they were in Rome (not 'be' or 'are,' but) turned from me" then; were "ashamed of my chain," in contrast to Onesiphorus; did not stand with me but forsook me (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2Ti 4:16</reference>). It is possible that the occasion of their turning from him was at his apprehension in Nicopolis, whither they had escorted him on his way to Rome, but from which they turned back to Asia. A hint to Timothy, now in Asia, not to be like them, but to imitate rather Onesiphorus, and to come to him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2Ti 4:21</reference>).<div eID="gen37598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Phygellus and Hermogenes--</hi>specified perhaps, as being persons from whom such pusillanimous conduct could least be expected; or, as being well known to Timothy, and spoken of before in conversations between him and Paul, when the latter was in Asia Minor. <div eID="gen37599" type="x-p"/>
entries.736b7a55b79abdb93373366042ed9911142f9f06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18183"/><div sID="gen37600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18183"/><hi type="bold">16. The Lord give mercy--</hi>even as Onesiphorus had abounded in works of mercy.<div eID="gen37600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the house of Onesiphorus--</hi>He himself was then absent from Ephesus, which accounts for the form of expression (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.19">2Ti 4:19</reference>). His household would hardly retain his name after the master was dead, as Bengel supposes him to have been. Nowhere has Paul prayers for the dead, which is fatal to the theory, favored by Alford also, that he was dead. God blesses not only the righteous man himself, but all his household.<div eID="gen37601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37602" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my chain--</hi>Paul in the second, as in his first imprisonment, was bound by a chain to the soldier who guarded him. <div eID="gen37602" type="x-p"/>
entries.882fd586ca3642eb33c395cd3205afa6ba2ff766: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18184"/><div sID="gen37603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18184"/><hi type="bold">17. found me--</hi>in the crowded metropolis. So in turn "may he find mercy of the Lord in that day" when the whole universe shall be assembled. <div eID="gen37603" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc73a25bb98c935c91a1ddcbba62b4d743124c4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18185"/><div sID="gen37604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18185"/><hi type="bold">18. grant unto him--</hi>as well as "unto his house" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16">2Ti 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>who rewards a kindness done to His disciples as if done to Himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.45">Mt 25:45</reference>).<div eID="gen37605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>from the Lord; "the Lord" is emphatically put instead of "from Himself," for solemnity and emphasis (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.5">2Th 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in how many things--</hi>"how many acts of ministry he rendered."<div eID="gen37607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts, so that the "ministered" may include services rendered to others as well as to Paul.<div eID="gen37608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">very well--</hi>rather as Greek, "Thou knowest better" (than I can tell thee, seeing that thou art more of a regular resident at Ephesus). <chapter eID="2Tim.1"/>

entries.7cfd285aa50f4f16b2312d75517fa316b92f1e55: <div eID="gen51949" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Timothy</title> <div sID="gen51950" type="x-p"/> In the preface to the first of these epistles, particular mention has been made of the parentage, country, and education of Timothy; his call to the evangelic office; and of his appointment to the presidency of the Church at Ephesus. And for every particular of this kind the reader is referred to that preface. What remains to be done in reference to the present epistle is to inquire into the time in which it was most probably written. The disagreement on this question among learned men is very great; some arguing that it was written about the year 61, others referring it to the year 66. Some asserting that it is the first, in order of time, of these two epistles; and that it was written on Paul's first imprisonment at Rome. Several of the most eminent critics are of this opinion; and they have supported their sentiments with arguments of no small weight. Hammond, Lightfoot, and Lardner, as well as several critics on the continent, contend for this earlier date. Macknight and Paley take the opposite side.
